On keeping a notebook of small failures

For about three years I have kept a paper notebook in which I write down every mistake that cost me more than an hour. Not the dramatic ones, which nobody forgets, but the small and slightly embarrassing kind: the afternoon lost because a configuration file was saved in the wrong folder, the meeting I prepared for on the wrong day, the bread that never rose because I had bought the wrong flour and refused to believe the label.

The habit started by accident. A colleague of mine, a careful and somewhat stubborn engineer, used to say that experience is only useful if you can find it again. She meant it as a complaint about our documentation, but the sentence stayed with me. Most of what we call experience is stored as a vague feeling that something will go wrong, without any record of why. The feeling is real, yet it is nearly impossible to hand to another person, and it fades faster than we like to admit.

Writing the failure down changes its character. On the page, a mistake stops being a private irritation and becomes a small piece of evidence. After a few months the entries began to repeat themselves. I noticed that a surprising number of them started with the words "I assumed". I assumed the train ran on Sundays. I assumed the backup had finished. I assumed the other team already knew. None of these assumptions was foolish on its own; each was reasonable, cheap to check, and unchecked.

There is a tempting conclusion here, which is that one should simply check everything. That is not what the notebook taught me. Checking everything is impossible, and people who try become slow and anxious. What the pages suggest instead is narrower and more practical: the costly assumptions cluster in a few predictable places. They gather around handovers, around anything scheduled on an unusual day, and around tasks that feel too simple to deserve attention. Knowing where the ice is thin is far more useful than walking carefully everywhere.

I have also learned to be suspicious of the entries that make me look good. Now and then I catch myself writing a failure in a way that quietly blames the weather, the software, or somebody else's unclear email. These are the least useful pages in the book. The entries that pay for themselves are the plain ones, written in the first person, with a time, a cause, and one sentence about what I would do differently.

A friend asked whether rereading the notebook is depressing. It is the opposite. The mistakes of two years ago look almost charming now, mostly because I no longer make them. The current ones are more interesting, and I expect that in two more years they will look charming as well. That seems to me a reasonable definition of progress: not the absence of error, but a steady improvement in the quality of one's mistakes.
